"We would support a framework on mandatory disclosures," OpenAI's Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon said at a hearing in Sydney. As OpenAI learned about the breach of the Australian health website and three other government websites, "we were trying to work through a process, we were trying to come up with a standard to apply", Kwon told the inquiry. "That is a function that a legal measure can provide. The representatives of society need to make more decisions so we are not making all these decisions." Anthropic has also had a number of incidents in which its agents have perpetrated hacks, and its head of policy for Australia and New Zealand, David Masters, also told the inquiry the company would be open to Australian laws requiring AI companies to disclose data breaches. In the US, federal legislation has been introduced that would require AI companies to report dangerous behavior such as attempts to evade human oversight. But there is currently no incident-reporting system that generally requires companies to disclose dangerous AI behavior when it is discovered. CONTENT CREATORS PUSH BACK Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles has said OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman didn't mention the breach of the Medicare system when the two met in early September. But Kwon told the inquiry Altman didn't know about the violation at the time, although it was known elsewhere within the company. "I agree that the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better, and we want to make sure something like that doesn't happen again," Kwon said. Anthropic's Head of Safeguards David Orr said his company had been running a "lengthy, deep investigation" since an OpenAI agent's hack of AI developer portal Hugging Face in mid-2026, and found no breaches of Australian government systems. At the inquiry, Australian content creators pushed back against attempts by AI companies to relax copyright laws which currently require the mostly foreign-domiciled tech companies to negotiate licensing deals before using their material for model training. Media reports have said the Australian government was considering an "opt out" clause for AI companies, effectively giving the AI companies access to content unless a rights holder objects. But that "places the burden on rights holders", said Kate Gilchrist, head of content and legal operations for national broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. "We cannot scour the internet and ensure that we are opting out on all those sites", she said. "The copyright system is completely adequate to manage the business of AI." The inquiry has hearings scheduled through to October 9 with a final report due November 30.

item.title: 英アストラゼネカ、米マサチューセッツ州に10億ドル投資へ 50％増員
item.description: [５日 ロイター] - 英製薬大手アストラゼネカは５日、総額５００億ドルの米国向け投資計画の一環として、東部マサチュー...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
英アストラゼネカ、米マサチューセッツ州に10億ドル投資へ　50％増員 9:11 配信

写真は英製薬大手アストラゼネカのロゴ。2021年5月、英マックルズフィールドで撮影。 REUTERS/Phil Noble

[５日 ロイター] - 英製薬大手アストラゼネカは５日、総額５００億ドルの米国向け投資計画の一環として、東部マサチューセッツ州に１０億ドル超を投じると発表した。今後数年で同州の従業員を５０％以上増やす見通し。

同社は既に同州ケンブリッジに新たな研究開発センターを開設した。詳細は以下の通り。

• 米ファイザー、イーライリリー、スイスのロシュなどの世界的な製薬会社はサプライチェーン（供給網）と国内生産能力の増強を図るため、製造と研究開発の強化に向け数十億ドル規模を投じて米事業の規模を拡大している。

• 同州のイノベーション拠点ケンドール・スクエアに建設された５７万平方フィート、１８階建ての施設では、がん、慢性疾患、希少疾患の治療法開発に加え、細胞療法の研究に力を入れる。

• アストラゼネカの近隣にあるゲノム医療拠点と合わせて、この施設には約２０００人の研究者や科学者が勤務することになる。

• 新しい研究センターにはロボット工学、自動化、人工知能（ＡＩ）を備えた実験室が１０フロアにわたって設置されている。

• ケンブリッジの拠点は北東部メリーランド州ゲイザースバーグにあるアストラゼネカのもう１つの主要研究センターに加わる。

• 同社は米国に２４カ所の研究、製造、営業、本社拠点を構え、２万５０００人超を雇用している。

item.title: ゴールドマン、米データセンター成長見通し維持 反対拡大でも
item.description: [５日 ロイター] - ゴールドマン・サックスは、米国のデータセンターに対する政治的な反対の高まりが急速な拡大に及ぼす...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ゴールドマン、米データセンター成長見通し維持　反対拡大でも 8:50 配信

米カリフォルニア州サンノゼにあるデータセンター。9月16日、サンノゼで撮影。REUTERS/Elizabeth Mendez

[５日 ロイター] - ゴールドマン・サックスは、米国のデータセンターに対する政治的な反対の高まりが急速な拡大に及ぼす短期的な影響は限定的で、２０２７年までの成長見通しはおおむね変わらないとの見方を示した。

４日公表のリポートで、米データセンターの２０２６年末時点の容量予想を５ギガワット（ＧＷ）引き上げて６４ＧＷとした一方、２７年末時点の予想は５ＧＷ引き下げて９０ＧＷとした。

• データセンターは人工知能（ＡＩ）モデルの学習や稼働に必要な計算能力を提供するが、電力需要や公共料金など地域への影響を巡る懸念から、全米各地で住民の反対に直面している。

• ゴールドマンは「米国のデータセンター開発は政界や地域社会からの反対が強まっているが、プロジェクトデータや当社の最新の容量推計は、２７年までの米データセンターの成長見通しがほぼ変わらないことを示している」とした。

• 米国のデータセンターの電力需要は２６年に３８％（１２ＧＷ）、２７年に３８％（１７ＧＷ）、それぞれ増加すると予測した。

• ６月のロイター／イプソス調査によると、米国でのデータセンター建設のペースを支持する米国民は３分の１にとどまる。

• メタ、アルファベット、アマゾン、マイクロソフト、ｘＡＩなどテクノロジー企業のＡＩ事業を支えるデータセンターが、自分の住む地域に建設されることを支持すると答えた人は１４％にとどまった。

• ゴールドマンは「世論も一段と否定的になっている」と指摘した。

• こうした反発は、１１月３日の米中間選挙を控える共和党にとって政治的な課題となっている。

item.title: ＮＺ企業信頼感、第3四半期も改善 燃料高でも楽観強まる
item.description: [ウェリントン ６日 ロイター] - 民間シンクタンク、ニュージーランド経済研究所（ＮＺＩＥＲ）が６日発表した第３・...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ＮＺ企業信頼感、第3四半期も改善　燃料高でも楽観強まる 8:46 配信

ニュージーランドのウェリントン市街。2025年9月、ウェリントンで撮影。REUTERS/Marty Melville

[ウェリントン ６日 ロイター] - 民間シンクタンク、ニュージーランド経済研究所（ＮＺＩＥＲ）が６日発表した第３・四半期の企業信頼感は改善した。燃料価格の上昇や地政学的な逆風が続く中でも、企業の楽観的な見方が強まった。

業況全般が改善すると回答した企業の割合が差し引き４３％と、前四半期の８％から上昇した。

調査は９月９─２８日に実施され、米国とイランの紛争が再び激化し、燃料価格が急騰した時期と重なった。

ＮＺＩＥＲは声明で「こうした最近の動向は、世界の原油供給と価格が依然として変動と不確実性にさらされていることを示しているが、景況感への影響は今のところ限定的なようだ」と指摘した。

季節調整済みでは、業況改善を予想する企業は４０％と、前四半期の１４％から上昇した。設備稼働率は９１．０％で、前四半期の９０．８％を上回った。

ＮＺＩＥＲは、今回の調査でコストと販売価格に関する指標が安定していることから、燃料高が幅広いインフレ圧力に波及するリスクは限定的だとの見方を示した。

item.title: Tsingshan’s Zimbabwe Steel Unit Partners With State Rail Firm to Boost Haulage Capacity
item.description: The Zimbabwean steelmaking unit of Chinese metals giant Tsingshan Holding Group has signed a partnership agreement with the National Railways of Zimbabwe to expand capacity to transport coal and steel, the state-owned rail operator said on Monday. The agreement covers the haulage of 1.1 million …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
The Zimbabwean steelmaking unit of Chinese metals giant Tsingshan Holding Group has signed a partnership agreement with the National Railways of Zimbabwe to expand capacity to transport coal and steel, the state-owned rail operator said on Monday.

The agreement covers the haulage of 1.1 million metric tons of coal from Hwange, about 600 km from Dinson Steel Company’s $1 billion plant in central Zimbabwe, which began production in 2024.

It also provides for the transportation of 600,000 tons of steel products from the plant to markets in Zimbabwe and elsewhere in the region, the NRZ said in a statement.

Grand Railway Solutions, a subsidiary of the Dinson group, will supply locomotives, wagons and fuel, while the NRZ will provide rail infrastructure and train crews.

The agreement includes a roughly $27 million upgrade of the 80-km railway line between Gweru and Mvuma, followed by the construction of a 50-km link between Mvuma and the steel plant under a build-operate-transfer arrangement.

Grand Railway Solutions will finance the new track, transfer it to the NRZ and recover its investment through offsets, the rail operator said.

“This deal is set to significantly increase annual tonnage for NRZ, while at the same time transferring the bulk of coal traffic from Hwange from road to rail,” the NRZ said.

The NRZ has struggled for years with inadequate government investment and has increasingly turned to partnerships with private logistics companies and bulk commodity customers to lift freight volumes.

Annual freight volumes fell to 2 million tons in 2025 from a peak of 12 million tons in the 1990s.

item.title: クアルコムによるアーム提訴の陪審審理開始、契約違反など主張
item.description:
Tom Hals Max A. Cherney Stephen Nellis
[ウィルミントン（米デラウェア州） ５日...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
クアルコムによるアーム提訴の陪審審理開始、契約違反など主張 8:39 配信

米半導体大手クアルコムのロゴ。2025年8月に撮影。 REUTERS/Dado Ruvic

Tom Hals　Max A. Cherney　Stephen Nellis

[ウィルミントン（米デラウェア州） ５日 ロイター] - 米半導体大手クアルコムが英半導体設計大手アーム・ホールディングスに対して起こした訴訟の陪審審理が５日、米東部デラウェア州の連邦地裁で始まった。長年対立してきた両社を巡る新たな法廷闘争で、クアルコムはアームが契約上で提供する義務を負っていた半導体の試験用ツールを提供しなかったほか、アームが２０２４年に重要なライセンス契約の打ち切りを通告した際、その情報をメディアに漏らして米メタ・プラットフォームズとの半導体取引を巡る協議に悪影響を与えたと主張している。

ソフトバンクグループ傘下のアームの大口顧客の１つであるクアルコムは今回の訴訟で、最長５年間にわたりアームへのロイヤルティー支払いを停止する権利を求めており、支払額は数十億ドル規模となる可能性がある。

クアルコム側のカレン・ダン弁護士は冒頭陳述で、同社が２１年に半導体新興企業でアームのライセンス保有企業だったヌビアを買収した経緯に言及。アーム幹部が社内文書でクアルコムを「敵」と呼び、ロイヤルティー収入が大幅に減少することを懸念していたことを示す文書があると説明した。

ダン氏は、アームがその後契約に違反するとともに、メタとの取引を含むクアルコムの事業関係を妨害し、メディアへの情報漏えいを組織的に行ったと批判した。

これに対しアーム側のグレッグ・ロカシオ弁護士は、クアルコムの主張が結局のところ、企業間の争いで訴訟を交渉材料として利用しようとするものだと反論。クアルコムが指摘するアームの行為によって、実際には何の損害も受けていないことを示す証拠を提示すると明言した。

またクアルコム側を支持する判断を下すには、アームの行為によって損害を受けたことをクアルコムが立証する必要があると裁判官から説明されることになると陪審員に説いて「彼らは少しも損害を受けていない」と述べた。

クアルコムが求める５年間のロイヤルティー支払い停止が認められれば、アームの売上高に大きな影響を及ぼす恐れがある。一方メアリーエレン・ノレイカ判事は、こうした支払い停止を定めた契約条項を無効とするかどうかを検討しており、無効となればクアルコムが請求できるのは、より少額の損害賠償に限られる可能性がある。

アームは契約違反を否定し、クアルコムの半導体取引にも損害を与えておらず、クアルコムが主張する取引自体についても、実現が確実ではなかったとしている。

さらにアームは、ライセンス契約終了通知の情報漏えいを理由にクアルコムが損害賠償を請求することもできないと主張し、クアルコム自身もアームを巡る独占禁止法当局の調査について、非公開情報をメディアに漏らしたと付け加えた。

陪審審理は５日間の予定で、両社の長期にわたる対立の新たな局面となる。

アームは数十年にわたり、クアルコムやエヌビディアなどの半導体メーカーに基盤となる半導体設計技術を提供してきた。一方、自社ブランドの半導体を投入するなど、顧客企業と競合する事業にも乗り出している。

ロイター 関連ニュース 中国テンセント、オラクルとＡＩチップ10万個のリース契約＝ＦＴ 東邦ＨＤ、ＰＨＣに初期的な買収提案＝一部報道で コラム：アーム株、法外な高値を維持できそうな訳 午前のドルは154円台に上昇、日米中銀会合前に方向感欠く アングル：超大型ＩＰＯラッシュ、ＡＩ相場は潮目変化か　日本株に波及リスク 最終更新: 10/6(火) 8:39 ロイター

item.title: Dozens quarantined in Siberia after plague institute lab worker dies
item.description: The World Health Organization said that based on available information, "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low".
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

Dozens quarantined in Siberia after plague institute lab worker dies

The World Health Organization said that based on available information, "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low".

This undated photo released by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, shows the institute workers in a lab. (File photo: AP/The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia/Far East)

MOSCOW: A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and the head of Russia's health watchdog to fly to the Irkutsk region. The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said on Monday (Oct 5) the situation was under control. The World Health Organization said that based on available information, "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low". New risk assessments would be conducted once further information became known, it said. US President Donald Trump said the death was a "big problem for Russia" and offered to help Moscow deal with it.

"We'll help," Trump said. "Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was closely monitoring the situation. Plague is endemic to Siberia - the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak - as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas.  However, it is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, though cases occur every year in other parts of the world - notably Africa. Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, prompts the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets. If identified quickly, it can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days. Local media have named the laboratory worker who died as Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. There were conflicting reports about how and where she fell ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia of as-yet unestablished origin.

AUTHORITIES SAY NO NEW CASES REPORTED, ALL CONTACTS TRACED Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, told state media the institute had not found evidence of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens after rumours spread on social media that the woman had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria. Nevertheless, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Siberia for an emergency meeting over the weekend. According to Russian media reports, about 200 people who had been in contact with the dead woman were quarantined, parts of the hospital in the town of Shelekhov where she died were cordoned off and an aluminium plant told its workers to wear masks. Rospotrebnadzor, in a later statement quoted by the TASS news agency, said officials in Irkutsk Region had found two cases of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with her. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted. Authorities urged people to remain calm and said there was no evidence that the woman's death was linked to her work. Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement that she had died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", adding: "Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified." He said the situation was under control and that all known contacts of the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.

item.title: Australian soldier killed, five injured when vehicle rolls over in training
item.description: An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured when a vehicle rolled over during a training exercise, the country's army said on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured when a vehicle rolled over during a training exercise, the country's army said on Tuesday. The Australian Army identified the soldier as Corporal Brendan Hannam, a father of two and an Afghanistan veteran. Hannam was a passenger in a vehicle that rolled over on October 5 at the Mount Bundey Training Area near Darwin, the Northern Territory's capital, it said. Of the five who were injured, two were in a stable condition in hospital in Darwin and three were being monitored at the army barracks. Lieutenant General Susan Coyle, chief of Australia's army, said Hannam was a "much beloved" soldier who had served on two operational tours to Afghanistan in 2019 and trained Ukrainians with the British Armed Forces in the UK. "His mates tell me that he would give the shirt off his back for anybody," Coyle told a news conference. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a post on social media the incident was a "terrible reminder of what families take on when their loved one bravely puts on our nation's uniform". It was the second death during training in recent months. An Australian Special Air Service Regiment soldier was killed during a parachute training exercise in May.

item.title: 米ＣＦＴＣ、暗号資産交換所向け連邦規制案 議会審議停滞で対応策
item.description:
Hannah Lang
[５日 ロイター] - 米商品先物取引委員会（ＣＦＴＣ）は５日、レバレッジを利用したデジタル資...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
米ＣＦＴＣ、暗号資産交換所向け連邦規制案　議会審議停滞で対応策 7:52 配信

暗号資産のイメージ。2025年9月撮影。 REUTERS/Dado Ruvic

Hannah Lang

[５日 ロイター] - 米商品先物取引委員会（ＣＦＴＣ）は５日、レバレッジを利用したデジタル資産取引を提供する暗号資産（仮想通貨）交換業者を対象とする新たな連邦規制の枠組みを提案した。暗号資産を包括的に規制する法案の議会審議が進まない中、現物取引市場の一部を連邦政府の監督下に置く狙いがある。

規制案によると、米国の暗号資産交換業者は、州ごとに異なる資金移動業者向け免許を中心とした現行の規制に代わり、ＣＦＴＣが監督する連邦レベルの規制枠組みを選択できるようになる。これはＣＦＴＣが従来から持つ、証拠金やレバレッジを利用した現物資産取引を監督する権限を活用する形。ＣＦＴＣはこれまで、規制上の位置付けが明確でない暗号資産の現物市場に対する監督権限を求めてきたが、その権限を明示的に付与できるのは議会に限られている。

セリグＣＦＴＣ委員長は５日、フォーダム大学ロースクールがニューヨークで開いたイベントで「金融の新たなフロンティアを切り開く起業家は長年、自分たちに市場での居場所があるのか不確実性に直面してきた。われわれはその答えを示す」と述べた。

規制案では、個人投資家にレバレッジ取引や証拠金取引を提供する交換業者について、ＣＦＴＣの監督を受ける新たな取引市場区分「暗号資産市場」を設ける。対象業者には相場操縦を防止する体制の整備や、保有する暗号資産などを裏付ける「プルーフ・オブ・リザーブ（準備資産証明）」が求められる。

ＣＦＴＣはまた、新たな区分の取引所で顧客が売買する際、登録済みの先物取引業者（ＦＣＭ）が仲介する仕組みを提案した。

規制案は具体的なレバレッジ倍率の上限を定めていない。一方、交換業者がレバレッジ取引を提供する場合、その商品についてＣＦＴＣ職員の承認を得る必要があるとしている。

今回の提案は、約２兆ドル規模の暗号資産市場に新たな規制を導入する包括法案「クラリティー法案」の議会審議が進まなかったことを受けた動き。同法案の柱の１つは、暗号資産の現物市場を監督する明確な権限をＣＦＴＣに与えることだった。

議会での審議停滞に伴って、暗号資産業界に融和的なトランプ政権の規制当局、とりわけ米証券取引委員会（ＳＥＣ）とＣＦＴＣが規制の明確化を進める役割を担っている。暗号資産業界はかねて、明確な規制ルールが必要だと訴えてきた。

ただアナリストからは、議会による法整備がなければ、規制は政権交代など政治情勢の変化や訴訟の影響を受けやすく、暗号資産業界を巡る法的不確実性が残るとの指摘も出ている。

ロイター 関連ニュース 〔アングル〕フライドバイ事件、操縦士襲撃後の急降下はまるで「垂直ジェットコースター」と専門家 焦点：空前のＡＩ投資、相応の経済効果実現へなお高いハードル アングル：暗号資産に迫る量子技術の脅威、解読リスク対策が業界の急務に アングル：米ＣＦＴＣ、仮想通貨無期限先物取引を完全承認か　業者は準備に奔走 コラム：金の安全性にテザー大量購入が影、暗号資産裏付け需要で異変も 最終更新: 10/6(火) 7:52 ロイター

item.title: US envoy attends event with Sudanese army chief in Egypt
item.description: An envoy of President Donald Trumpsaid he attended an event over the weekend with the head of Sudan's army, which is fighting a war with paramilitary forces that has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
item.dc:creator: Kanishka Singh
item.content:encoded: An envoy of President Donald Trump said he attended an event over the weekend with the head of Sudan's army, which is fighting a war with paramilitary forces that has created one of the world's [USN:L6N45M0KU TEXT:"worst humanitarian crises"]. DETAILS: US Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos said on X he attended a lunch hosted by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi alongside Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. "We ... reaffirm the United States' continued efforts, alongside our Egyptian partners and our other regional and international partners and allies, to advance a political solution to the crisis," Boulos added in his post. A senior official in Sudan's military-led government said Burhan had a "casual encounter" with Boulos, but the two did not hold any talks. The event in Egypt came less than two weeks after Washington [USN:L6N45E0RI TEXT:"withheld a visa"] for the Sudanese army chief ahead of a scheduled UN appearance, in a move that Sudanese and other sources said was linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal that Khartoum has resisted. Sudan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule. The US State Department said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary nor either of their respective leaders "represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan". The war has displaced more than 14 million people and unleashed waves of ethnically driven killings . "The United States stands ready to support all efforts leading to a comprehensive dialogue among the Sudanese political forces, leading to a preliminary road map of the future of the Sudan," Boulos said on Monday. Washington [USN:L6N45M0KU TEXT:"has accused"] the RSF of committing genocide and the army of carrying out war crimes. Both have previously denied abuses.

ORLANDO, Florida, Oct 5 : The Nasdaq surged to a fresh high on Monday, as earnings optimism and lower oil prices offset rising bond yields. The biggest moves of the day were in Brazilian assets, which logged historic gains after right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro's strong showing in the first round of voting in the presidential election suggests he is a strong favorite to win the second and decisive round in three weeks. In my column today, I look at when traders and financial TV anchors on the NYSE floor should start ordering their "S&P 10,000" caps. That milestone is only 30 per cent from current levels, and if Q3 earnings are anywhere near as strong as Q2, it suddenly won't feel too far away at all. Today's Key Reads • Spain's Sanchez gambles on snap election after housing protests give rare boost

• Right-wing wave in Brazil's Congress boosts Bolsonaro camp ahead of presidential runoff • What will Washington do next if US bond yields keep rising? • US goes into midterm elections with a less dynamic form of full employment • EU risks becoming sick man of the world if it doesn’t reform quickly: Mike Peacock • Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: Brazil +8 per cent, biggest rise this century outside GFC and pandemic. Nasdaq +1 per cent to new high, S&P 500 +0.7 per cent, Dow +0.2 per cent.SECTORS/SHARES: Every sector on the S&P 500 rises except real estate. Comms services, materials +1.2 per cent. Nvidia +2 per cent to new record high, market cap closing in on $6 trillion.FX: Brazilian real +4 per cent, biggest rise in 4 years. Euro -0.3 per cent to 17-month low. Dollar index hits 18-month high.BONDS: French/German spread narrows 5 bps. US yields rise, 10-year and 30-year highest closes in over two decades.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil -2 per cent, gold little-changed above $4,100/oz. Today's Talking Points: Brazil That rumbling you feel beneath your feet is the first tremors of what could be a political earthquake in Brazil. Right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former hard-right President Jair Bolsonaro, did much better than expected in the first round of voting in Sunday's presidential election, and from a financial markets viewpoint at least, the verdict is clear — the sizzling rally in Brazilian assets on Monday says it all. Incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the left-wing veteran going for his fourth non-consecutive term, is considering tapping Vice President Geraldo Alckmin to be his next finance minister if re-elected, in a bid to bolster his fiscal credibility and win over centrist voters. But it may be too little too late — online betting markets are pointing to an 83 per cent likelihood that Bolsonaro wins in the second round of voting. Europe To France, Italy and Germany last week, investors can add Spain to their European political risk watch-list, after Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election following nationwide protests over housing. It's a high-stakes gamble for Sanchez, whose Socialist Party trails in nearly every opinion poll. Defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last remaining left-leaning governments at a time when the far right is making unprecedented gains across the region. Spain's political turmoil isn't tied to fiscal concerns like other countries — Spain is one of the fastest-growing economies in the euro zone, its deficit is around 2-2.5 per cent of GDP, and yield spreads are under relative control. Still, markets are twitchy — Spanish yields rose 5 bps and the euro slumped to a fresh 17-month low around $1.12. Dollar In G10 FX, the big beneficiary of deepening political and bond market uncertainty sweeping, to varying degrees, across Europe, the UK and Japan is the dollar. The US doesn't have its political, debt or bond market troubles to seek either, of course. But to coin an old FX market adage, the greenback is once again proving to be the cleanest dirty shirt in the laundry. This isn't what President Trump or Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent really want. They would prefer a weaker dollar that is more competitive in the global marketplace, which would theoretically help boost US exports and narrow the trade deficit that Trump says is a result of America being "ripped off" by the rest of the world. On the other hand, a stronger dollar helps suppress imported price pressures and the need for tighter monetary policy. Now that's music to Trump's ears. What could move markets tomorrow? • Germany industrial orders (August) • Euro zone retail sales (August) • US trade (August) • US Treasury sells $58 billion of 3-year notes at auction • US Federal Reserve officials scheduled to speak include New York Fed's John Williams, Dallas Fed's Lorie Logan, and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman Want to receive Trading Day in your inbox every weekday morning? item.title: Jeffrey Archer, UK novelist and scandal-plagued politician, dies on eve of final book
item.description: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, died aged 86 on Monday, just one day before his final novel "Adam and Eve" was due to be published.
item.dc:creator: Sam Tobin
item.content:encoded: Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, died aged 86 on Monday, just one day before his final novel "Adam and Eve" was due to be published. The confidant of former prime minister Margaret Thatcher lived a life that swung from the heights of luxury and fame to the lows of a two-year stint in prison for perjury over paying a woman for sex. He sold more than 300 million copies of his books, spent a total of five and a half years on the New York Times bestseller lists and found fans around the world with his pacy thrillers, among them the 1976 debut "Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less" and 1979's mass-selling "Kane & Abel". Publisher HarperCollins said Archer, who had met and signed books for fans in London's Leicester Square Theatre on Sunday and had been scheduled to speak at events this week, died "suddenly and peacefully at home ... between writing sessions". "We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend," said Kate Elton, HarperCollins' UK CEO and Archer's editor. "When he set out to write 'Adam and Eve', he told me from the very beginning that it would be his final novel". HEAVY DEBTS CURTAILED HIS LIFE AS A LAWMAKER Archer first made headlines when he entered parliament in 1969, aged 29, before he became a casualty of a fraudulent investment scheme which meant he did not stand for re-election in 1974 but went into writing to try to clear his debts. "When I was three, I wanted to be four; when I was four, I wanted to be prime minister," he was quoted as saying in 2001. Despite only a short stint in parliament, he remained a central figure within the Conservative Party, spent more than 30 years sitting in the upper House of Lords chamber in parliament and raised millions of pounds for charity. Cabinet ministers and celebrities flocked to his "champagne and shepherd's pie" parties, with guests recalling how anyone looking for the bathroom at his London apartment was told to "Go past the Picasso and turn left at the Matisse". Some of that interest waned with his very public downfall. In 1987, Archer sued the Daily Star tabloid for saying he had paid a woman for sex, winning a then-record £500,000 ($660,450) in damages. The case returned to the public eye when he was selected as the Conservative candidate to become London's first elected mayor in 1999. A former friend accused him of lying and Archer was eventually charged with perjury and perverting the course of justice, convicted and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He served two years, during which time he wrote "A Prison Diary". ARCHER TRIAL NOTORIOUS FOR JUDGE'S SUMMING UP The trial became notorious for the judge's summing up of evidence given by Archer's wife Mary. "Remember Mary Archer in the witness box," the judge, Bernard Caulfield, told the jury. "Your vision of her will probably never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance?" And, of Archer, he added: "Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel?" The fall from grace did no harm to his literary career. HarperCollins said Archer's books were sold in 119 countries and he was due to speak at an event in London on Wednesday and the Cheltenham Literature Festival this weekend. Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the Conservatives, said she was shocked by the news, having received a message from Archer as she attended her annual party conference on Monday morning saying: "great outfit, great speech, no need to reply". Asked recently by the BBC why he wanted "Adam and Eve" to be his last book, Archer said: "It's been 50 very happy years. But there is always a time. I think the clever thing in life is when to get out." ($1 = 0.7571 pounds)

Oct 5 : Wall Street equities were buoyed by advances in mega-cap stocks on Monday, as Treasury yields held near multiyear highs, the dollar advanced against the euro, and oil prices relented. US stock indexes were supported by heavyweight technology companies such as Nvidia , Meta Platforms , and Microsoft . The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.18 per cent, the S&P 500 added about 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained about 1 per cent, touching a fresh record high.  European shares closed higher even as French equities slid to a six-month low on fiscal concerns and Schneider Electric fell after acquiring US software firm PTC. The pan-European STOXX 600 <.STOXX> index ended 0.4 per cent higher, after hitting a four-month low last week as global bond yields surged on inflation, higher corporate bond issuances and worsening fiscal outlooks.  Latin American markets also climbed, led by a rally in Brazilian stocks and the real currency, after right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed poll predictions in the first round of the presidential election and advanced to a runoff against leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe rose 0.7 per cent.  "Relative equity market calm amid the bond market’s 'perfect storm' is understandable, given accelerating economic growth and the AI boom’s rate insensitivity," Lisa Shalett, chief investment officer of Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, said in an email. Shalett wrote that her team was watching three areas for signs of stress: equity market and earnings revisions breadth; high-yield bond spreads; and US dollar strength along with currency market volatility. FRANCE WEIGHS ON THE EURO The euro recovered some ground to trade at $1.122 after falling by as much as 0.8 per cent to a 17-month low of $1.1160.       The single currency, down about 2.5 per cent last month, has come under pressure as investors fret over France's rising debt and political gridlock ahead of next year's presidential election. The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over safer German debt surged above 150 basis points on Friday, fueling concerns of broader contagion across European markets. "France is the real deal in terms of risk premia for the euro," said Saxo strategist Neil Wilson, noting that French government plans to reduce the budget deficit still face parliamentary scrutiny and could ultimately be watered down. French 10-year yields stayed below Friday's peak of 4.993 per cent, while German yields were also little changed.  The euro's slide lent fresh support to the dollar, which also drew strength from elevated Treasury yields. The dollar index rose 0.2 per cent. The dollar's resilience suggests it "may be too soon to write off" its long-term role, BlackRock Investment Institute strategists wrote in a note on Monday. They added: "With markets pricing more Fed tightening than we think will materialize, there is limited scope for a sustained dollar bull run." Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields rose 3.4 basis points to 5.31 per cent. Borrowing costs across major economies remain near multiyear highs as deteriorating public finances, heavy debt issuance and elevated energy prices continue to pressure bond markets.   FED REPRICING OFFERS SUPPORT Figures released last week showed US job growth slowed more than expected in September and payrolls for the previous two months were revised sharply lower, prompting investors to largely rule out a Federal Reserve rate increase this month. Japan's Nikkei rose 2.4 per cent and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose 1.3 per cent.  Investors see a roughly 24 per cent chance of a Fed rate increase this month, down from 64 per cent a week ago, according to CME FedWatch data, though a move in December remains largely priced in. Oil prices fell on Monday after crude exports from the Middle East increased and the Group of Seven nations pledged to boost supplies, though selling was limited by ongoing disruption fears linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran. Brent crude futures settled $1.93, or 1.89 per cent, lower at $100.32 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude lost $1.68, or 1.84 per cent, at $89.43. Spot gold was steady at $4,143 an ounce.

McDonald's hit with class action alleging AI-powered menu price-fixing

File photo. People walk by a McDonald's in New York City, US, Aug 17, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Jordan Tovin)

FAST

WASHINGTON: McDonald's has been sued in federal court in Chicago in a proposed nationwide class action alleging the fast-food company illegally coordinates menu prices across its franchises and company-owned restaurants through an AI-powered pricing system. The lawsuit, filed on Friday (Oct 9), said McDonald’s violated US antitrust law by conspiring with independent franchisees to fix prices using algorithms trained on nonpublic data.  Reuters reported last week that McDonald’s pricing engine uses machine-learning algorithms to continually analyse data from millions of daily transactions across its nearly 14,000 restaurants. The lawsuit cited the Reuters article, which said other fast-food companies are also turning to AI to help with pricing and other operations.

"Independent businesses must set their prices independently," the lawsuit said.  McDonald’s, in a statement on Monday, called the allegations speculative and uninformed. "AI does not set the price of a Big Mac or any other menu item," the company said. It said franchisees make their own pricing decisions, and that the use of pricing recommendation tools and analytics is widespread across industries.  US plaintiffs have filed a wave of class actions in recent years alleging that companies used algorithms or AI to illegally coordinate prices for hotel rooms, apartment rentals and other purchases. Lark Turner, a lawyer for the plaintiff, said in a statement, that McDonald's is "leveraging its troves of data and its franchised system to nickel-and-dime consumers down to the last French fry". The plaintiff, an Illinois resident, is seeking to represent a class of potentially millions of McDonald's customers, the lawsuit said.

item.title: French bond contagion fears are rattling the euro
item.description: A sliding euro is the latest alarm bell for policymakers facing a surge in French borrowing costs that has started to spill over into the broader euro area.
item.dc:creator: Dhara Ranasinghe, Alun John
item.content:encoded: A sliding euro is the latest alarm bell for policymakers facing a surge in French borrowing costs that has started to spill over into the broader euro area. The euro hit [USN:L1N45R03D TEXT:"17-month lows below $1.12"] on Monday and tumbled against sterling , the Swiss franc and Japan's yen . France is at the heart of the European market concerns. The French government is seeking to enact an unpopular [USN:L1N45N0A3 TEXT:"2027 budget"] to lower its deficit and contain its record-high debt load, a tall order in a deeply divided parliament as political factions position ahead of next year's presidential election. Investors, unwilling to take chances, are [USN:L8N45O0S7 TEXT:"dumping French bonds"] while buying safe German debt. With the premium investors demand to hold French over German government bonds now at its [USN:L8N45O0YO TEXT:"highest since"] the 2010-2012 euro zone debt crisis, currency markets fear contagion. At stake is feeble economic expansion in a bloc rocked by political uncertainty. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party last month suffered the worst regional election defeat in postwar Germany. And on Monday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"snap election"]. Italy also holds elections next year. With inflation already rising on soaring energy costs and higher yields increasing household and corporate borrowing costs, further euro weakening could leave the European Central Bank caught between fighting inflation and calming bond markets. The French/German 10-year bond yield gap last week saw its biggest weekly jump in decades, while the gap between Italian and German yields hit almost 130 basis points (bps), posting its biggest weekly rise since the COVID-19 crisis. "The bond sell-off is seeing bigger moves in anything that is perceived in any way, shape, or form as more vulnerable, and that has seen an outbreak of euro selling that's gathered momentum," said Societe Generale's chief FX strategist Kit Juckes. "The factors that held euro/dollar above key levels through the summer... I think that's gone," he said, pointing to earlier assumptions of a short-lived energy shock and a US push to weaken the dollar. NEW DIMENSION TO EURO WEAKNESS While the euro is comfortably above 20-year lows hit in 2022 when Russia's invasion of Ukraine sparked an energy crisis, the bond market moves add a new dimension to euro weakness. Every further 10 bps widening in the French spread against Germany would be associated with a 0.4% fall in euro/dollar, BofA FX strategists estimate. "The typical response is closer to zero most of the time, but (the spread impact) can rise significantly in times of acute stress," Goldman Sachs analysts said in a note. "Spreads do not matter for the currency until they are the only thing that matters," they said, adding that the impact on the euro rises when a risk event pushes German yields down, but those elsewhere in the bloc higher. This was the case last week when Germany's Bund yield fell almost 17 bps, its biggest weekly drop since 2024 . "Euro/dollar is usually influenced more from the dollar side, but this time there is an impact from Europe too," said Amundi Asset Management's head of global FX Andreas König. "You have to go back a bit in time to when European headlines last made the euro move," he said. König did not see a turnaround in the medium term and was sticking with a dollar overweight position given the US growth and rate outlook. CFTC positioning data show traders positioned for a fall in the euro, a view also reflected in currency options. Three-month euro risk reversals , which reflect the difference between the cost of an option to buy the euro against the cost of one to sell it, fell on Friday to their most bearish since 2024. Analysts said the euro could test $1.10, while SocGen's Juckes also highlighted euro vulnerability against the likes of the yen and Swiss franc. The euro fell almost 4% against the yen in September. A falling currency alongside bond market stress means talk has turned to how policymakers could stabilise markets, especially if 2027's French election causes more strain. The ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument allows it to buy an unlimited number of bonds from a country experiencing an "unwarranted, disorderly" tightening of financing conditions. For now, growth, though weak, has strengthened. Euro zone business activity expanded at its fastest pace in nearly 3-1/2 years in September, S&P Global data showed. The degree to which banks, the main financiers of companies in the region, can keep lending to their economies is also in focus. "If the fiscal contagion risk in Europe is not contained, I can see euro/dollar trading lower, despite the fact that it was already slightly undervalued," said Stephen Jen, CEO and co-CIO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management.

item.title: Cenovus strikes $5.7B deal to buy Athabasca Oil, expand production
item.description: Cenovus Energy said on Monday it would buy Athabasca Oil in a $5.7 billion (US$4 billion) cash-and-stock deal, cementing its position as one of Canada’s largest oilsands producers at a time the ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Cenovus Energy said on Monday it would buy Athabasca Oil in a $5.7 billion (US$4 billion) cash-and-stock deal, cementing its position as one of Canada’s largest oilsands producers at a time the country is aiming to boost crude output. The acquisition of Athabasca — one of the last remaining independent companies in Alberta’s increasingly consolidated oilsands sector — comes a year after Cenovus’ $8.6 billion purchase of MEG Energy. The deal highlights a stronger growth outlook from Canadian oilsands companies in the wake of sweeping regulatory and policy changes by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government aimed at removing barriers to investment by fossil fuel producers. It adds about 45,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day to Cenovus’ thermal oil sands production, and the company said the assets could be expanded to produce 115,000 barrels per day by 2032. Cenovus’ total upstream production in the second quarter of 2026 was approximately 970,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. The transaction, expected to close in December, will also give Cenovus full ownership of Athabasca’s subsidiary Duvernay Energy, strengthening its position in the oil-rich Kaybob Duvernay area, where it sees potential to grow output to 20,000 boepd. Shares of Cenovus were down 2.8 per cent in morning trading, while Athabasca shares jumped 14.3 per cent to C$12.17 following the roughly $12-per-share offer, a 13.4 per cent premium to the stock’s last closing price on Friday. Cole Smead, CEO of Smead Capital, who owns Cenovus shares in his portfolio, described the company’s move as aggressive and said it was paying a high price for the assets. But he also said it spoke to Cenovus’ confidence in its ability to advance proposed new oil sands growth projects at Athabasca’s Corner and Leismer sites. “It’s an expensive move, but it’s an optimistic move,” Smead said. “If they’re going to go out and grow production at Athabasca, it means they like the future.” Cenovus CEO Jon McKenzie told analysts on a conference call that Cenovus is contemplating advancing the Corner project three years earlier than Athabasca’s existing development plan, to produce approximately 40,000 bpd by 2032. Carney said last week his government will fast-track the approval process for a new 1-million-bpd proposed crude oil export pipeline to the Pacific coast, which could allow Canadian oil sands producers to significantly expand production. But Canada’s largest oilsands companies, including Cenovus, have not yet made a final investment decision to go ahead with a large-scale carbon capture and storage project that Carney has said is a condition of the new pipeline going ahead. Athabasca shareholders will receive 0.264 Cenovus shares for each share held, valuing the deal at about C$5.76 billion, according to a Reuters calculation based on Athabasca’s 480.34 million shares outstanding per data compiled by LSEG. (Reporting by Pranav Mathur in Bengaluru and Amanda Stephenson in Calgary; Editing by Shreya Biswas, Shinjini Ganguli and Nia Williams)

item.title: Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after injuring spectator with ball
item.description: Russian Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final clash with Novak Djokovic after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd, striking a spectator in the eye.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russian Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final clash with Novak Djokovic after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd, striking a spectator in the eye. World number five Medvedev was trailing 7-5 5-3 on Monday and had lost a point when he hit the ball coming off the wall. The spectator, who was sitting in the first row behind Medvedev, clutched his left eye and appeared to be in pain as he walked out of the gallery, assisted by stadium staff. Medvedev did not protest the umpire's decision to disqualify him. The Russian will lose his points and prize money from the tournament as a result of the default. "Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all," Medvedev told reporters." I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels." The 30-year-old former US Open champion said he did not cause the incident intentionally. "The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don't think I was ever close to such a situation." Sixth seed Djokovic said he was shocked by the incident. "I hope that person is not badly injured," said Djokovic, who was disqualified from the US Open in 2020 in similar circumstances. "On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match." Both semi-finals ended prematurely in Beijing as Hubert Hurkacz retired with an adductor injury earlier in the day. Australian Alex de Minaur was leading the first semi 6-4 3-2 when his Polish opponent, who had struggled with movement throughout the match, retired. 'GRUELLING BATTLE' Djokovic's win extended his China Open record to 33 victories without a loss, extending his record of making the best start in a men's singles tournament in the Open Era. The Serbian beat French and U.S. Open champion Alexander Zverev [USN:L6N45Q056 TEXT:"in the quarter-finals"] to break the record Rafael Nadal set by winning his first 31 matches at Roland Garros. Djokovic, 39, survived punishing long rallies and saved seven break points to take the first set in one hour and 19 minutes. He was serving for the match when Medvedev was disqualified. "It was a gruelling battle ... it always is a big battle with Daniil and it's so hard to play him," said Djokovic, who won the tournament all six times he played in it from 2009 to 2015 before returning to the event this year. "Another final. There's something about Beijing that just keeps me going."

item.title: Nutrien to shut Trinidad Nitrogen operations amid gas supply constraints
item.description: Canadian agrichemical company Nutrien said on Monday it will indefinitely shut its Trinidad Nitrogen operations at the Point Lisas facility after a review of strategic alternatives, citing ongoing ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Canadian agrichemical company Nutrien said on Monday it will indefinitely shut its Trinidad Nitrogen operations at the Point Lisas facility after a review of strategic alternatives, citing ongoing natural gas supply constraints and uncertainty in the country. The decision comes nearly a year after Nutrien began a controlled shutdown of the facility on October 23, 2025, citing port access restrictions imposed by Trinidad and Tobago’s National Energy Corporation and a lack of reliable and economic natural gas supply. Nutrien said those challenges had reduced the free cash flow contribution from its Trinidad operations over an extended period, leading it to determine that an indefinite shutdown was the best course of action. The world’s largest potash producer said the move was expected to improve its free cash flow and the return on invested capital. Nutrien said the shutdown would not affect its 2026 nitrogen sales outlook, with its North American operations expected to meet customer demand. The company produced about 85,000 metric tons of ammonia and 55,000 metric tons of urea per month at its Trinidad operations. (Reporting by Varun Sahay in Bengaluru; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli)

item.title: BT’s vulture M&A dials up a worthwhile connection
item.description: The £20 bln UK telecom group said it had bought loss-making TalkTalk out of administration. Boosting its already big market share raises antitrust risks, yet the UK government’s blessing may help. A lowball price, plus likely synergies, means shareholders may not be left hanging.
item.dc:creator: Neil Unmack
item.content:encoded: Allison Kirkby is looking like Britain’s answer to Jamie Dimon. The BT (BT.L) CEO has just stepped in to buy up the carcass of indebted telecom group TalkTalk, just as JPMorgan (JPM.N) boss is known for saving weak US banks. It looks like a risky move: TalkTalk is lossmaking, and the deal could raise antitrust risks, although Kirkby’s shareholders can probably emerge happy. TalkTalk may create a new motto in European leveraged finance: never lend to UK telco buyouts. The group was already in turnaround mode when Toscafund took it private in 2020: it relied heavily on the BT-owned network Openreach to sell broadband, giving it little pricing power in an increasingly competitive market. In recent years, high debt and dwindling customers has seen its profitability collapse. It had been kept afloat by chief lender Ares Management (ARES.N) , which has over the years put over £500 million in debt and equity into the group. TalkTalk’s dire financial status made rescuing it increasingly challenging. Any buyer would have needed to fund operating losses, invest in new customer service, and pay arrears and future network charges to Openreach. That makes BT a logical acquirer, as more than half of TalkTalk’s revenue goes straight to Openreach, which would be lost if the group went bust. The outlay for BT is around £400 million, including the non-receipt of some £100 million of Openreach charges. The remainder will go to Ares, which will recover some £100 million in high-ranking senior lending and more in fees, and asset-backed lender KKR (KKR.N) . It will also cover costs. But the rest of TalkTalk’s debt, which Fitch Ratings estimates at £1.5 billion in total, will face steep losses. TalkTalk's 8.25% bond, issued in 2025, was trading at just 2 pence in the pound on Monday. Buying TalkTalk out of administration makes sense, but it’s still risky for Kirkby. BT’s share of the UK retail market may now exceed 35%, raising the risk that the UK Competition and Markets Authority unwinds the deal or forces disposals. Prime Minister Andy Burnham appears to have panicked at the prospect of 1 million customers losing broadband access overnight if TalkTalk went into liquidation, and granted a public interest intervention notice, which should tame the CMA. Still, rival operators will petition for remedies: Virgin Media 02 has called the deal a “ stitch-up ”. The deal maths looks sound for BT, providing some cushion. It can make savings by slashing costs and selling more products. Assume synergies of perhaps half Talk Talk’s operating costs, equivalent to £150 million pounds, and the savings' present value alone, after tax and capitalised on a multiple of 10, would exceed £1 billion, more than double the initial outlay. And saving TalkTalk avoids the risk of BT's broadband customers vanishing or going to a rival. The TalkTalk saga may prompt changes. A clearer administration regime should allow ailing broadband providers to avoid the risk of customers being switched off. And broadband companies may need to operate with lower debt. BT may benefit from the deal, but in an ideal world the telecom group should never have needed to step in in the first place. Follow @Unmack1 on X. BT Group on October 5 announced it had bought the main businesses of the TalkTalk group out of administration. The transaction, which will see BT take on TalkTalk’s 1.5 million retail customers, will result in a “cash impact” of £400 million, BT said in a statement. That figure includes the “non-receipt” of £100 million owed to BT by TalkTalk. BT shares rose by 1.7% to 199 pence as of 1046 GMT on October 5. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Oil's new problem isn't supply. It's logistics
item.description: Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the [USN:S8N43Z003 TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"] – despite the continued threat of Iranian attacks. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses. Crude flows through the embattled waterway reached 14.2 million barrels per day on a seven-day average on Sept. 26, nearly 80% of pre-war levels, according to analytics firm Kpler. While volumes have declined since, they will likely be revised higher because ships often disable satellite tracking systems while traversing the strait and for several days thereafter. Either way, the trend is clear: a lot more crude is getting through the strait. So why is Brent still trading above $100 per barrel? In a word, logistics. For decades, the global oil industry functioned as a finely tuned system designed to move enormous volumes of crude and fuels over long distances at the lowest possible cost. The conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe have fractured that model, as a combination of record-high tanker rates, soaring insurance costs and a severe shortage of refining capacity has created bottlenecks across the energy supply chain. Those problems may take months, if not years, to unwind, leaving consumers facing persistently high energy bills – even if the crude supply squeeze continues to ease. BREAKING THE BLOCKADE Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz following the onset of the war with the US and Israel on February 28 rapidly reshaped global oil flows. Gulf producers diverted supplies through alternative routes, buyers sought barrels from more distant regions and governments released unprecedented volumes of oil from strategic reserves. One of the biggest changes was that Saudi Arabia – previously the world’s largest oil exporter – diverted its exports through its [USN:L4N45E0KG TEXT:"East-West pipeline"], which delivers crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. At one point this year, 4% of global oil supplies were via this route. However, after the pipeline came under attack by Iranian-backed Iraqi militias [USN:L6N4590XN TEXT:"in early September"], Saudi Arabia was forced to redirect exports back to the Gulf via Hormuz, which it discovered, could be more easily transited than previously thought. Saudi exports through Hormuz averaged 3 million bpd in September, the highest level during the conflict, according to Kpler. While Saudi Arabia’s crude exports through Hormuz in September were still only around half of pre-war volumes, the Kingdom’s exports could quickly near pre-war levels as the East-West pipeline [USN:L4N45E0KG TEXT:"gradually returns"] to normal operations. Ironically, then, the attack on the East-West pipeline, which was intended to cripple Riyadh, may have instead weakened Tehran's most powerful leverage – its purported control of the Strait – by demonstrating that large volumes can still transit Hormuz and other major export hubs despite continued attacks. GREAT FREIGHT Yet the recovery remains fragile. On the one hand, the increase in Gulf exports has helped reduce the global oil deficit. Energy Aspects estimates the market now faces a shortfall of around 1.6 million bpd, down from roughly 4 million bpd during the peak disruption in May. Under normal circumstances, such an improvement in supply would exert significant downward pressure on prices. Instead, Brent remains above $100 a barrel, more than 40% above pre-war levels. Prices certainly reflect a substantial risk premium linked to the possibility of renewed escalation, as Washington and Tehran have still failed to reach any form of understanding over the future of Hormuz. But geopolitics is only part of the story. Freight and insurance costs, once a relatively minor component of the delivered price of oil, have become major price drivers. This is partly due to the current [USN:L6N45A0SP TEXT:"shuttle system"] operating around the Gulf. Multiple tankers are frequently required to transport crude though Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman, where cargoes are transferred to smaller vessels before heading to buyers in Asia. This ties up significant numbers of very large crude carriers (VLCCs), reducing vessel availability elsewhere. At the same time, buyers are increasingly sourcing crude from the Atlantic Basin and shipping it to Asia over longer routes, further tightening tanker supply. The result has been a surge in key tanker rates to record highs. Rates to transport crude from the Middle East to Asia aboard a VLCC recently exceeded $1.2 million per day, up from roughly $30,000 a day in January, according to shipping broker Poten & Partners. As a result, freight costs that once accounted for around 3% of the delivered price of a barrel now represent roughly 27%. These costs are unlikely to normalise until trade flows return to something resembling their pre-war pattern. Indeed, a further recovery in exports through Hormuz may initially worsen the situation by increasing demand for the elaborate shuttle networks now required to move crude safely through the region. REFINING CRUNCH The loss of refining capacity in the Middle East and Russia, where Ukrainian drone attacks have crippled dozens of plants, has compounded the problem, particularly for diesel. Diesel prices have surged to record highs, becoming a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"major political concern"] for U.S. President Donald Trump ahead of next month's midterm elections, as diesel powers much of modern industry, agriculture and manufacturing. The Group of Seven's decision last week to [USN:B5N44301Y TEXT:"release diesel"] from strategic stocks will likely provide only temporary relief as it does nothing to restore lost refining capacity. What’s more, refiners are increasingly competing for the medium-sour crude grades that generate higher diesel yields. Those barrels are concentrated in the Middle East and Russia, precisely the regions where supply disruptions remain most severe. That dynamic is creating a feedback loop. Tight refining capacity boosts diesel prices, which increases demand for diesel-rich crude grades, which in turn supports crude prices. The result is that oil prices are no longer primarily a function of supply, but of the industry's ability to transport and process crude – making it much more challenging to bring these prices down. (The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso , a columnist for Reuters.) Enjoying this column? item.title: OpenAI's Altman says AI benefits warrant accepting some risks
item.description: Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public "We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded. Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding: "I think there's a lot of daylight." "I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, 'This technology is going to get so powerful, and it's so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,'" Altman said. He called that "a completely unacceptable trade-off" that runs counter to the "lighter-touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI. "I wouldn't take a trade of saying, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" Altman said. "Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff." Altman's remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry [USN:L6N45L0PN TEXT:"to slow down"] to "pace the frontier," a stance that Altman publicly endorsed. Anthropic researcher [USN:L6N45A0PY TEXT:"Jacob Coxon"] resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it "could kill us all by the end of the decade. Reuters reported in September that Anthropic warned that, despite AI's potential benefits, the technology can sometimes act in ways that run counter to its makers' intentions and penetrate other companies' systems. The company said advanced models could exhibit [USN:L6N45L00I TEXT:""self-preserving behaviors,""] including attempts to "resist shutdown," "conceal or manipulate information," or generate outputs that could be interpreted as "coercive, deceptive, or manipulative." However, US President Donald Trump has largely [USN:L6N45O0XQ TEXT:"dismissed calls"] for new restrictions, arguing they would make it harder for American companies to compete with Chinese rivals. He has repeatedly said existing law enforcement agencies, including the Justice Department, provide sufficient safeguards and that no new rules are needed.

item.title: Evacuated in an incubator, now back in Gaza getting to know mama
item.description: Bissan was born because of an airstrike.
item.dc:creator: Nidal Al-Mughrabi, Mahmoud Issa
item.content:encoded: Bissan was born because of an airstrike. Two weeks into the war in Gaza in October 2023, an Israeli attack ripped through her family's home in Beit Lahiya near the Israeli border, killing a sister she never got to meet. The blast seriously injured her pregnant mother, who was forced to deliver Bissan six weeks early to save both their lives. Weeks later, the baby was driven out to Egypt in an ambulance while still in an incubator, one of a group of 29 preterm infants evacuated from a neonatal hospital ward as Israel's invading forces drew close. Seven of those babies died in Egypt, but Bissan survived. While she grew in Egyptian hospitals and a care home, her mother, Sundus al-Kurd, never lost hope that they would be reunited. Back in Gaza, as the war raged on, Sundus made video calls to speak to the baby whenever she had internet access. In March this year, with a ceasefire ostensibly in place, Bissan was returned to Gaza to be reunited with her family in a mission assisted by the UN, along with 10 other children from the same group evacuated as preterm babies. When they were finally reunited, Bissan didn't recognise her mother, Sundus said. The girl, now 2-1/2, would say "mama" to any woman who showed her kindness. Reuters documented their reunion and visited with them and several of the other children in the months that followed as they built bonds with their mothers and fathers. Here are their stories. GETTING USED TO EXPLOSIONS Returning to Gaza as a toddler meant learning to live in a war zone, where Israeli airstrikes have continued despite the ceasefire agreed a year ago between Israel and Hamas. When Bissan first heard the booms, she would freeze in a state of fear for several minutes, Sundus said. She still begins to panic if a balloon pops near her. "Her life changed. Her life became sleeping and waking up to the sound of explosions, to the sound of the numerous attacks and missiles," said her mother. On a sunny morning soon after their reunion, her mother took her to a small zoo in central Gaza. Bissan, who wears pink-framed glasses, gazed in awe as a blue parrot latched onto her mother's arm. 'HE WAS SUPPOSED TO CALL ME DAD' Of the 11 preterm babies evacuated to Egypt in November 2023 and returned to Gaza this year, not all were able to meet their mothers. For baby Ibrahim it was already too late. His mother, Israa Badr, fell into a deep state of depression after her son, born during her eighth month of pregnancy, was evacuated to Egypt. She died the following month. Her husband Jabri Badr said doctors "told us she died of sorrow, of sadness." "Ever since he was in her womb, she thought about him, dreamed of holding him, playing with him, and feeling what it was like to be a mother," he said. Ibrahim is now reunited with his father in Gaza, but Badr said they have struggled to connect. "He was supposed to call me dad. Today he doesn't even say dad, or anything. I tell him to come, and he ignores me." Arafat Abu Mashayikh, a Gaza-based mental health expert, said that after two years apart it was natural that it would take time for parents to connect with their children. MOTHER'S MILK, AND HER EMBRACE Bissan, Ibrahim and the others "were deprived not only of their mother's milk but also of her embrace and the emotional development that comes with it," Abu Mashayikh said. Rebuilding the bond takes time. Some days, Bissan and Sundus walk down to Gaza's Mediterranean shore. On a recent afternoon, they held hands as they walked where the sand meets the sea. Bissan flashed a big smile as she gazed out to the horizon. The evenings are more difficult, but still bring them closer together, Sundus said. When explosions ring out in the middle of the night, Bissan wakes up and seeks out her mother's care. "Bissan has begun to understand who mama really is, who her mother really is," Sundus said. "I am the only person present in her life. I am the one who feeds her, changes her clothes, combs her hair, and plays with her."

item.title: UK's Nest pension picks Wellington in £3.5 billion emerging market active equity shift
item.description: Britain's largest workplace pension scheme Nest plans to move its entire £3.5 billion ($4.6 billion) in emerging market equities to US active manager Wellington Management, ending a focus on index investing to better manage sustainability risks, an executive told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Simon Jessop
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 1 story has been corrected to say that Nest plans to move, not has moved, in paragraph 1.) Britain's largest workplace pension scheme Nest plans to move its entire £3.5 billion ($4.6 billion) in emerging market equities to US active manager Wellington Management, ending a focus on index investing to better manage sustainability risks, an executive told Reuters. Nest, the £68 billion scheme into which more than 14 million workers are automatically enrolled, had invested the money passively for more than a decade, echoing a global market trend in which trillions of dollars have followed suit to save on fees. After awarding its first emerging market passive mandate to Northern Trust in 2014, Nest moved to the manager's Climate Aware Emerging Markets Equity Strategy in 2021. Doing so left the scheme with a smaller stake in more than 1,000 stocks, limiting its ability to engage with firms on climate change, diversity, workers' rights and other sustainability issues that could impact long-term returns. By moving to a more focused portfolio of around 100-150 stocks, the scheme hopes to better influence governance at the companies, Rachel Farrell, Nest's director of public and private markets, said in an interview. "A pure passive approach... just wasn't engaged enough," Farrell said. "We weren't really spending time understanding each of the stocks that we would own in our members' portfolios." "To influence as a shareholder, you need to be an important owner of that particular company," she added, without disclosing the costs of making the switch. WIN FOR WELLINGTON The decision is a big win for US investor Wellington, which manages $1.3 trillion in assets, of which $44 billion is in emerging market equities. Farrell said the decision to move the mandate followed a periodic internal review begun in 2024, and that the passive strategy had met its return objectives, without disclosing details. The new strategy will be benchmarked to the MSCI Emerging Market index and Wellington will target an additional 100 basis points in outperformance, Farrell said. "Emerging Markets is one of the markets that is somewhat less efficient," she said. "There is evidence that an active manager can add value." BULLISH EMERGING MARKETS The MSCI Emerging Market index is up 22% year to date, outperforming the developed market MSCI World Index, which is up 9%. Emerging market demand picked up in the second half of 2025 following large outflows since 2021, fund firm Ashmore said in a February report, in which it put total EM equity assets at $1.4 trillion, equivalent to the market value of automaker Tesla. Nest has around 5.2% of its assets in emerging market equities with the bulk in a systematic developed markets strategy. The decision by Nest follows a move last year by the People's Pension to move its index-tracking emerging markets equity allocation to a more active quantitatively driven strategy. A third of Britain's working population is currently invested with Nest and that is expected to grow to half of the workforce by 2030, Nest said. Taking in around £700 million a month, total assets will near £100 billion by 2030, it added. ($1 = 0.7542 pounds)

item.title: TSMC evaluates potential Texas investment, sources say
item.description: Taiwan's TSMC , the world's largest contract chipmaker, is evaluating a potential investment in Texas to expand chip production in the US, two sources familiar with the matter said.
item.dc:creator: Wen-Yee Lee, Fanny Potkin
item.content:encoded: Taiwan's TSMC (2330.TW) , the world's largest contract chipmaker, is evaluating a potential investment in Texas to expand chip production in the US, two sources familiar with the matter said. The potential investment would be in addition to the $265 billion TSMC has already committed to Arizona, one of the sources said. The plans have not been finalised, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. Taiwanese media first reported the development this week, citing unnamed industry sources. TSMC declined to comment. The company unveiled in July a [USN:L1N43I00B TEXT:"further $100 billion"] investment in Arizona, expanding its previously pledged investment there to $265 billion to build semiconductor manufacturing facilities. Chief Executive C.C. Wei said at the time that "probably additional four or more fabs will be built," referring to both front-end and back-end facilities. Including current and planned projects, TSMC's Arizona operations will comprise 12 fabrication and advanced packaging facilities as well as an R&D centre. Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang [USN:L4N43J03M TEXT:"told Reuters"] in July that the company would continue to invest in the United States.

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: L'Europe ouvre dans le vert, accalmie sur l'obligataire
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: L'Europe ouvre dans le vert, accalmie sur l'obligataire 6 octobre (Reuters) - Les principales Bourses européennes avancent mardi en début de séance, soulagées par une accalmie sur le marché obligataire, tandis que les investisseurs restent attentifs à la dépréciation de l'euro. Le français BPCE acquiert une participation de 7% dans la banque espagnole Sabadell MADRID, 6 octobre (Reuters) - Le groupe bancaire français BPCE a acquis une participation d'environ 7% dans la banque espagnole Sabadell par le biais d'achats sur le marché et d'instruments financiers, avec l'intention de devenir un actionnaire à long terme, ont annoncé mardi les deux établissements. Carine Damois nouvelle directrice financière de Renault, Duncan Minto s'en va 5 octobre (Reuters) - Renault Group a annoncé lundi la nomination au poste de directrice financière de Carine Damois, qui succède à Duncan Minto à un moment charnière pour le groupe au losange. Schneider Electric chute en Bourse après l'annonce du rachat de PTC pour €20,2 mds Schneider Electric chutait de quelque 9% lundi en milieu de matinée à la Bourse de Paris, après l'annonce de l'acquisition de 100% du capital du spécialiste des logiciels industriels américain PTC sur la base d'une valorisation à 22,6 milliards de dollars (20,2 milliards d'euros). Les marchés brésiliens attendus en hausse après la percée de Flávio Bolsonaro SÃO PAULO/BRASÍLIA, 5 octobre (Reuters) - Les marchés brésiliens devraient rebondir lundi après la performance surprise de Flávio Bolsonaro au premier tour de la présidentielle dimanche, selon des analystes interrogés par Reuters. Le sénateur de droite a recueilli 47% des voix, contre environ 45% pour le président sortant Lula, que les sondages donnaient en tête avec trois points d’avance. L'ascension de Revolut, devenue une rivale des grandes banques européennes, valorisée €103 mds LONDRES, 5 octobre (Reuters) - La fintech britannique Revolut s'est hissée au rang de start-up la plus valorisée d'Europe, posant un défi pour les grandes banques classique au vu de sa croissance fulgurante en un peu plus de 10 années d'existence. La reconstitution des stocks de brut et de carburant pourrait prendre deux ans, selon le PDG d'Aramco LONDRES, 5 octobre (Reuters) - La pénurie de pétrole brut et de carburants raffinés devrait s'aggraver, et la reconstitution des stocks mondiaux, puisés à titre de mesure d'urgence, pourrait prendre deux ans, a déclaré lundi Amin Nasser, directeur général de Saudi Aramco , lors de la conférence Energy Intelligence à Londres. La Première ministre s'engage à respecter une discipline budgétaire TOKYO, 5 octobre (Reuters) - La Première ministre japonaise Sanae Takaichi, s'est engagée lundi à "maîtriser" les émissions obligataires et à agir rapidement face aux turbulences du marché, cherchant ainsi à rassurer les investisseurs inquiets de la détérioration des finances publiques du pays. Air Liquide monte en Bourse après son nouveau plan stratégique 5 octobre (Reuters) - Air Liquide a annoncé lundi anticiper une progression annuelle moyenne de son chiffre d'affaires de 5% d'ici à 2030, avec une variation de plus ou moins un point de pourcentage par rapport à cette moyenne projetée, et a lancé un programme de rachat d'actions de quatre milliards d'euros. L'euro à un creux de 17 mois, les difficultés budgétaires en France font craindre un effet de contagion SINGAPOUR, 5 octobre (Reuters) - L'euro est tombé lundi à un creux de 17 mois face au dollar américain sur fond de difficultés budgétaires en France qui suscitent les craintes d'une contagion dans le reste du bloc monétaire après les fortes tensions observées la semaine dernière sur le marché obligataire.

item.title: How is the Nobel Peace Prize decided?
item.description: The Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on Friday. Here is a look at how the award works:
item.dc:creator: Gwladys Fouche
item.content:encoded: The [USN:L6N45F0CZ TEXT:"Nobel Peace Prize"] will be announced on Friday. Here is a look at how the award works: WHO IS NOMINATED? [USN:L8N3YV0R0 TEXT:"Some 287 candidates"] have been nominated, including 208 individuals and 79 organisations. We don't know who because the list is kept secret for 50 years, inside a vault in the basement of the Norwegian Nobel Institute in Oslo. Still, nominators, of whom there are thousands worldwide, can choose to reveal their choices. IS US PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP NOMINATED AND CAN HE WIN? The leaders of [USN:L6N3TZ12B TEXT:"Cambodia"], [USN:S0N3OK054 TEXT:"Israel"] and Pakistan have said they nominated Trump, though there is no way of verifying that. If Trump is nominated, [USN:L6N45F0CZ TEXT:"his chances to win are very low"], according to experts. WHO ARE THE FAVOURITES THIS YEAR? [USN:L8N45D0ES TEXT:"Pope Leo"], the [USN:L6N3V50RZ TEXT:"International Criminal Court"], the [USN:L6N3YV0K0 TEXT:"International Court of Justice"] or [USN:L6N41D1BE TEXT:"Francesca Albanese"], the UN special rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories. Also possible are [USN:L6N40Y0KB TEXT:"Emergency Response Rooms"], a Sudanese network of community groups providing aid during the civil war, or non-governmental organisation Save the Children, for helping children in the conflict. Outsiders include the International Space Station, as an example of what countries can achieve even when they are at odds with each other. The US, Russia and Europe work together on the ISS. WHO DECIDES? The Norwegian Nobel Committee consists of five individuals appointed by the Norwegian parliament. Members are often, but not always, retired politicians. The current committee is led by the head of the Norwegian branch of PEN International, a group defending freedom of expression. Another member is an academic. They are all put forward by Norwegian political parties and their appointments reflect the balance of power in Norway's parliament. WHO CAN WIN? The short answer is: [USN:L6N45D0OK TEXT:"whoever fits the description"] set out in the 1895 will of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel. It says the prize should go to the person "who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses". The more complicated answer is that the prize "needs to be placed in the current context", according to Kristian Berg Harpviken, the award committee's secretary, who prepares the work for the award body. He participates in the deliberations but does not vote. "They will look at the world, see what is happening, what are the global trends, what are the main concerns, what are the most promising processes that we see," he told Reuters last year. "And processes here can mean anything from a specific peace process to a new type of international agreement that is under development or that has recently been adopted." WHO CAN NOMINATE? Thousands of people worldwide can propose names: members of governments and parliaments; current heads of state; university rectors, professors of history, social sciences, law and philosophy; and former Nobel Peace Prize laureates, among others. Nominations closed on January 31. Members of the committee can make their own nominations too, no later than at their first meeting in February. HOW DOES THE COMMITTEE DECIDE? The committee discusses all the nominations, then establishes a shortlist. Each nominee is then assessed and examined by a group of permanent advisers and other experts. The committee meets roughly once a month to discuss the nominations. The decision tends to be taken in August or September, said Harpviken. The committee seeks to reach a consensus on its selection. If it cannot, the decision is made by majority vote. The last time a member quit in protest was in 1994, when Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat shared the prize with Israel's Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin. WHAT DOES THE LAUREATE GET? A gold medal, a diploma, 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million) and immediate global attention. WHEN ARE THE ANNOUNCEMENT AND THE CEREMONY? The announcement will take place on October 9 at the Norwegian Nobel Institute in Oslo and is made by the committee's chair. The ceremony takes place at the Oslo City Hall on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. ($1 = 9.8283 Swedish crowns)
